item.title: Democrats Need Big Margins in Houston. Can This Progressive Deliver?
item.description:
Dr. Letitia Plummer rallied her Democratic campaign volunteers on a recent afternoon with a blunt message: The battle for Texas may come down to Harris County, which includes Houston.

“We’ve got to perform at a certain level to make sure we can flip the state,” Dr. Plummer, who is running for the top county position, known as county judge, told the volunteers standing in the shade of a live oak.

About one in six Democratic votes in Texas has come from Harris County in recent elections, according to official results, making the county critical to the party’s hopes of winning a statewide race for the first time in decades.

Dr. Plummer, a dentist and former Houston City Council member, narrowly won a primary against Annise Parker, a former mayor favored by moderates. She is running to succeed Lina Hidalgo, who is not seeking re-election as county judge.

Democratic strategists said candidates like Dr. Plummer could energize the party’s base. She has strong support among her fellow Black Democrats and Houston progressives and has been backed by Representative Jasmine Crockett, who lost to James Talarico in the Senate primary. Ms. Crockett campaigned alongside Dr. Plummer on the first day of early voting this month, stopping at several polling centers.

“It’s sending a message about how integral Harris County is going to be,” Ms. Crockett said in an interview during one of her stops, in northeast Houston.

That fact has not been lost on Republicans.

Led by Gov. Greg Abbott, Republicans have spent tens of millions of dollars this year to win back the county. The governor has vowed to turn Harris County into a Republican bastion again or at least come close enough to thwart Democrats like Mr. Talarico.

Mr. Abbott was in Harris County on the first day of early voting, rallying supporters at a country-style restaurant on the west side of the county.

“We’ve got to fight together,” Mr. Abbott told the cheering crowd. “We will win this election, we will destroy the Democrats, and we will keep Texas Texas.”

Dr. Plummer has an unusual background for a countywide position in Texas: If elected, she would be the state’s highest-ranking Muslim woman in office. Her father, also a dentist in Houston, converted to Islam to marry her mother, who was from Zanzibar.

Dr. Plummer’s identity has attracted attacks in a year when anti-Muslim rhetoric has been a prominent feature of Republican messaging across Texas. Text messages sent to Republicans in Harris County have warned of a Muslim “takeover” and urged people to support her opponent, Orlando Sanchez.

“Say ‘No!’ to sharia law,” read one message from a Republican donor, Steve Hotze. “Elect Orlando Sanchez for Harris County Judge.”

Dr. Plummer said her faith, “just like anyone else’s faith, has no bearing on my ability to serve,” adding that the county “deserves better than politics built on hatred, intimidation and division.”

Mr. Sanchez said in an interview that he did not support “that type of rhetoric,” but that he could not control what others said.

Democratic strategists said the party needs margins in Harris County and other urban areas that can overcome Republican support in the state’s vast expanse of rural areas and small towns.

“The path to statewide victory runs through Harris County,” said Katherine Fischer, director of the Texas Majority PAC, which is working with the Texas Democratic Party on organizing and voter turnout.

The Democratic Party wants to maintain control of the levers of power in local offices like county judge. The position oversees emergency management and leads the county’s commissioners court, which votes on the budget and other policies.

Dr. Plummer appears to have the inside track, according to the few public polls. Mr. Sanchez has conceded that the political environment has been difficult.

“It is like swimming upstream in a Category 3 rapid,” Mr. Sanchez, a former county treasurer, said in the interview.

Both candidates remain relatively unknown among voters. A University of Houston survey this month found that nearly half of respondents did not know enough about either candidate to have an opinion.

In her primary, Dr. Plummer ran as an unapologetic progressive, a contrast with statewide candidates like Mr. Talarico, who have aimed more for the center and, in the general election, courted independents and wavering Republicans.

Mr. Sanchez, who moved to Houston from Cuba as a child, has presented himself as a pragmatic conservative, similar to the kind of Republicans who used to hold sway in Harris County. He has tried to win over voters by focusing on issues like reducing crime, curbing spending and lowering property taxes.

“It’s intellectually dishonest to talk about affordability and then hammer the local citizens” with tax increases, Mr. Sanchez said.

Dr. Plummer has also vowed to stop property tax increases, to address crime while improving jails, and to focus on reducing flooding — a perennial problem. She has stressed “affordability and access and equity.”

“We’ve got to level the playing field,” she said in an interview.

Democrats hope they can exceed their high-water mark in Harris County in 2018, when they got 58 percent of the vote in the race for U.S. Senate. Since then, Republicans have been gaining ground, nearly winning several countywide races in 2024.

But unlike statewide Democratic candidates such as Mr. Talarico, Dr. Plummer is not focused on winning over Republicans this year. “This is a turnout game,” she said. “This is how many Democrats can you get to the polls.”

On a recent afternoon, Dr. Plummer heard about flooding and residents’ desire for more regular police patrols as she went door to door in a mostly Black neighborhood south of downtown. She also ran into a few people who knew her personally — a former patient of her father’s and a breeder who once sold her a miniature poodle puppy.

“People are struggling nowadays — the gas, the food, housing, rent,” the dog breeder, Paula Haywood, 61, said as she stood on her porch. She said she would be supporting Dr. Plummer.

“She’s out here working,” Ms. Haywood said. “We listen to the one that’s out there for us.”

Dr. Plummer’s volunteers included a retired teachers-union worker, Frank Pratka, 70, who wore a hat with a pin for the Houston chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.

“A lot of people tense up when you say ‘socialism,’” he said. “I like Letitia. I’m tired of Texas always being red. It’s embarrassing.”

item.title: Voters Usually Ignore Corruption as an Issue. It Now Has Their Attention.
item.description:
Like many Americans, Michael Nave has a hunch that politicians of both parties enrich themselves while the working class struggles to make ends meet.

But on Wednesday, Mr. Nave, a Republican, decided the party in power has become too corrupt. He cast his vote early, in Clearwater, Fla., against every Republican on the ballot, including Representative Anna Paulina Luna, who has been depicted by her opponent as emblematic of a party rife with self-enrichment and cronyism under the leadership of President Trump.

“Trump said he would drain the swamp, and he’s become the swamp,” said Mr. Nave, 61, of Dunedin, Fla.

Allegations of corruption in Washington are nothing new in political campaigns. They are usually shrugged off by voters who figure all politicians are equally guilty, whether they be Democrats such as former Senator Bob Menendez of New Jersey or Republicans like former Representative George Santos of New York. But Democratic efforts to bolster the issue this year may be resonating amid a drumbeat of stories about Mr. Trump’s staggering increase in wealth and the billionaire and corporate elites who have supported him.

Some recent polls have shown corruption has risen to the top of issues that voters say they care about most, fueled by a withering distrust in government and a sense of opacity in Washington.

“How can you always trust what’s behind a closed door?” asked Karen Jarrett, 58, who lives in Tennessee, a quick drive from the state line with Mississippi. She added, “People’s eyes are wide open now.”

But such sentiments may go only so far amid greater worries about inflation, war and personal security.

“It didn’t click with me,” Juan Pino, 51, a cook in Florida, said of corruption. He voted straight Democratic because, he said, he always votes that way.

Democrats are certainly trying to drive home the issue by tying politicians’ self-enrichment and insider trading to the soaring cost of living. Republicans, too, including Ms. Luna, are seeking to capitalize on corruption as a campaign theme.

And for some voters, it seems to be sinking in more than ever.

“It’s more out in the open now,” said Steve Wiegard, 46, who works with a fire safety company in Olive Branch, Miss. “I think about it every day.”

The word has become a constant refrain in campaign ads from both parties, even if the definition of corruption has at times been stretched. A political action committee supporting Democrats this week launched the latest corruption-themed attack ads, including one highlighting stock trades by Representative Victoria Spartz of Indiana and her family, which the ad says accompanied “policies that make life more expensive” for voters.

A committee supporting Republicans this month launched an ad labeling Troy Jackson, the Democrat challenging Senator Susan Collins of Maine, “too corrupt” for the state because his son is a lobbyist.

Corruption now seems to include secretive nondisclosure agreements struck with data centers, the war in Iran, even the gerrymandering of Black-majority districts after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act.

“We have politicians trying to pick the voters instead of voters picking the politicians,” said Chaz Molder, the Democratic mayor of Columbia, Tenn., and a House candidate who saw his home drawn out of the Middle Tennessee district where he was running. “That is corrupt.”

The most recent entrant: Democratic efforts to clog Alaska’s four-person ranked-choice ballot with candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, including one challenger named Dan Sullivan.

In the Tampa Bay region of Florida, corruption has emerged as central to the race between Ms. Luna and Leela Gray, a Democrat and retired Army brigadier general. Voters in the newly redrawn district overwhelmingly supported Mr. Trump in 2024, but Democrats hope to flip the seat by tying Ms. Luna to the president and portraying her as a glamorous partygoer, currying favor with wealthy donors.

One ad for Ms. Gray called Ms. Luna “part of the problem in D.C., including the culture of corruption,” highlighting allegations in the media that she gave insider information to a Republican influencer who then placed a bet on a political prediction market.

Ms. Luna has denied the report, sent a cease-and-desist letter to her opponent’s campaign over the ad and noted a Justice Department letter that confirmed she is not under investigation. In turn, Ms. Luna has sought to portray Ms. Gray as compromised because she owns stock in Big Pharma, companies building data centers and big banks buying up single-family homes.

In an interview, Ms. Luna said she has led the fight on corruption by seeking to restrict stock trading by members of Congress. “The only reason this is a national discussion is because I forced it,” Ms. Luna said.

In interviews at early voting sites with more than two dozen voters in Ms. Luna’s district west of Tampa, most agreed corruption is a problem in both parties, but many shrugged off relentless attacks as par for the course.

James Shively, the owner of a landscaping company, said both parties were untrustworthy. He voted Republican because, he said, “Democrats are socialists.” Jonathan Castro, a human resources specialist with no party affiliation, voted for Democrats because he believes Trump’s immigration enforcement policies are too draconian.

Neither said his vote hinged on corruption.

For Jeff Davis, a Republican retiree, corruption was a bank shot in his congressional choice; he said he had voted against Ms. Luna because she supports Mr. Trump, who he believes is corrupt.

Marc Bachyrycz, a personal trainer with no party affiliation, cast his ballot for Ms. Luna because like him, she is an Air Force veteran. He also appreciated that while in office, she tried to crack down on congressional stock trading.

“No party is without fault, but at least she’s trying to do something,” Mr. Bachyrycz said.

For some voters, the issue is breaking through, even if it’s not decisive.

“I know insider trading has always gone on, but I think now it’s way worse,” said April Robinson, 52, an independent who voted along with her husband for Ms. Gray. “They are purposefully manipulating the markets.”

To others, the tried-and-true of their preferred party still holds sway. Joelle Eden, 57, a former Democrat who switched parties a decade ago, voted Republican because she believes the party prioritizes public safety and border control.

“I just want to make sure the country is safe,” Ms. Eden said.

Curt Anderson and Anastasia Economides contributed reporting.

item.title: How Disabled Children Were Caught Up in Trump’s Homeless Crackdown
item.description:
On the campaign trail, Donald J. Trump vowed to send homeless people “back to mental institutions, where they belong.”

It was characteristically blunt and provocative, yet it tapped into a widespread sense of frustration in America over the rise in visible homelessness.

But the Trump administration’s efforts to chip away at constitutional protections for people who live on the street and struggle with mental illness and addiction could also have consequences for a much bigger group: millions of people living with disabilities who are not homeless.

In a memo in June, the Justice Department asserted a new interpretation of a decades-old Supreme Court decision that has required the government to provide care to people with significant disabilities in their own communities whenever possible, rather than segregating them in institutions.

That Supreme Court decision put in place new limits and obligations and changed what it means to live with a disability in America — whether you’re a homeless person with mental illness, a preschooler with cerebral palsy or a nursing home resident with Alzheimer’s.

Now, many families caring for someone with a significant disability see an emerging threat to government obligations they have long relied on.

Those obligations include public benefits that the administration has sought to limit in other ways, like Medicaid. In one case in Florida, the Justice Department already appears to be using its reinterpretation of the law to argue that the government is not required to provide at-home care for children with complex medical conditions.

More such cases could follow, potentially upending the way people with disabilities receive care in any number of states. Among the many people who could be affected by the Florida case is a 13-year-old boy named Dylan Webb who has A.D.H.D. and autism, as well as a blood-clotting disorder and a heart condition that requires constant access to a defibrillator.

For several hours a day, a nurse is with Dylan to help his parents and teachers keep him safe. “We are very aware that his risk of sudden death is there, which is why we really don’t take our eyes off of him,” his mother, Kayla Webb, said.

At school and at home in the Jacksonville suburb where the family lives, the nurse manages Dylan’s many medications and makes sure that the feeding tube he uses is clean and that he is eating and drinking exactly enough.

The staffing of Dylan’s nurses is governed by a court order that covers thousands of children in Florida with complex medical needs. It emerged from an anti-discrimination lawsuit, one of many where the federal government pressed states to do more to prevent disabled people from being put in institutions.

At a trial in 2023, the federal judge in Florida, Donald Middlebrooks, heard stories of enormous hardship. One grandmother testified she had lost her home because, with patchy nursing care for the grandson who lived with her, she couldn’t work consistently. In a decision ordering more in-home nursing, the judge wrote that when nursing shifts went unfilled, families endured harrowing conditions trying to keep their children from growing up in pediatric nursing homes.

But the Justice Department is seeking to undo the judge’s order in Florida, citing the legal position on disability rights that the office took in the June memo, when it said states were not required to provide care for disabled people at home and in their communities whenever possible.

Asked to respond to questions about the government’s approach to homelessness and to concerns that the Justice Department’s new position was putting some people at risk, Kiersten Pels, a spokeswoman for the Department of Justice, said the opinion “could help homeless individuals with mental illness get the help they need.” But she said that would ultimately depend on decisions by individual states, and she did not respond to follow-up questions about how exactly the opinion could help people receive treatment.

The fight over services for people like Dylan is the latest development in a decades-old reckoning over how to support people with disabilities.

For more than a century, state-run institutions housed people with severe mental illness and intellectual and developmental disabilities. Most were shuttered after reports of systemic abuse and mistreatment outraged the country.

The disability rights movement surged, leading to new civil rights laws and eventually the Supreme Court’s 1999 ruling, Olmstead v. L.C. The justices found that housing people with disabilities in institutions when they could otherwise receive care outside in the community was illegal discrimination.

But the resources to integrate disabled people as fully as possible have chronically fallen short of the needs in many places.

Julia Graff, who litigated Olmstead cases for almost 10 years before leaving the Justice Department in 2025, said that there had always been bipartisan support for her team’s work.

“And I think that’s because it affects people of various political ideologies pretty equally, and if you live long enough, disability comes for us all,” Ms. Graff said.

That history didn’t stop the Justice Department from reversing its long-held approach to disability rights.

Soon after returning to the White House last year, President Trump issued an executive order telling officials that homeless people should be put in institutions for treatment, a break from the general practice of trying to provide treatment where they live. It asked the attorney general to seek the reversal of court precedents that stood in the way.

The shift began in earnest in June, when the Department of Justice issued the opinion announcing its new position that Olmstead had been misinterpreted again and again by lower courts.

Since then, lawyers for the Justice Department have been working to carry out the opinion in civil rights cases that reach beyond the homeless population.

Where it had previously accused states of unlawfully segregating people with disabilities in nursing facilities, the Justice Department is now pulling out of cases and asking judges to end settlements.

In Florida, lawyers asked a court to undo the order that affects Dylan’s family.

In Texas, lawyers got a judge’s blessing to alter a set of federal disability regulations by wiping out references to the integration mandate.

Funding and services for people with disabilities are expected to decline with the cuts to Medicaid spending President Trump signed into law last year.

Jennifer Mathis, deputy director of the nonprofit Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law, said that she worried states struggling to manage with less Medicaid money could see the Justice Department’s retreat from enforcement as permission to cut supports for people of all ages with all kinds of disabilities.

“I think it will mean that people will become homeless, people’s lives will fall apart, people will lose their jobs,” she said.

On the opposite side are some think tanks that have questioned the reach of Olmstead. One of those organizations is the Cicero Institute, which has had a significant role in shaping the Trump administration’s homelessness policy.

Devon Kurtz, who leads Cicero’s homelessness work, said state leaders were frustrated by how the power of Olmstead protections defined how they provide treatment.

“This isn’t a red-blue issue,” he said, adding, “blue states get sued under Olmstead just as much as red states.”

The Trump administration has stood by its efforts to reassess Olmstead.

“Nothing about the amount of care has changed,” said Lauren Bis, a spokeswoman for the White House. “States are now empowered to provide Americans with the appropriate care they need.”

The future remains uncertain for the families at the heart of the Florida nursing case.

If the court order were undone, said Lindsey Weinstock, who represented the Department of Justice in the trial against Florida, “I don’t trust that things aren’t going to backslide.”

The toll might not be immediately apparent. But parents and caregivers say they would absorb the impact through each unfilled shift, with sleep, work and their own health all suffering.

Ms. Webb, 37, struggles with a number of chronic illnesses and said she and her husband were worried about a backup plan for Dylan’s care. Her son’s medical team has told Ms. Webb that they could think of only one facility in the country that might accept him and be able to meet his needs, and it’s in Rhode Island.

“I said, ‘So he has better luck getting into Harvard,’” Ms. Webb said.

“If we really do take away community-based and home-based services,” she said, “there is no place for him to go.”

Kitty Bennett and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: A Spirited History Lingers in the Capitol’s Haunted Halls
item.description:
In the dark of night in 1862, a watchman stationed at the United States Capitol saw two glowing eyes.

The orbs came closer, and grew bigger. The watchman stopped cold. He thought the creature was a cat, but as the animal galloped closer, it ballooned to the size of an elephant. The feline pounced, and the guard fired at the figure before it disappeared.

“The eyes of this elephantined alley trouper are supposed to glow with all the hue and ferocity of the headlights of a fire engine entering one of Washington’s notoriously dark alleys,” The Washington Post wrote of the tale some 73 years later.

So began the legend of the demon cat.

For more than a century, myths of a ghoulish feline and other poltergeists haunting the halls of Congress have made ghosts a fixture of Washington folklore, and given the Capitol a little-known distinction as America’s marquee haunted house.

There is the tale of the slain former congressman who still trips reporters on the marble steps inside the Capitol to avenge his murder by a journalist. A construction superintendent is said to have cursed the Capitol in his final breath as he was being crushed by the ceiling of the Old Supreme Court Chamber. Even John Quincy Adams, who in 1848 suffered a stroke and died at the Capitol, is said to have been spotted on many a late night passing through the building to give a speech he never got to deliver.

The ghost stories, chock-full of embellishment, are likely more fiction than fact. But they have staying power, serving as a bridge between today’s Capitol and those who once walked its halls. Perhaps that is why the spirited fables resurface every year around this time, almost as sure as the leaves will fall.

After all, it is Halloween on the eve of a midterm election.

Many of the stories date to the Civil War period, when the bloody conflict lured many people to spiritualism, a practice of communicating with other realms, said A.J. Orlikoff, the director of programming at Congressional Cemetery, which lies about two miles southeast of the Capitol and is filled with the graves of 19th-century lawmakers.

Back then, prominent political figures engaged with the spiritualist movement, including President Abraham Lincoln and the first lady, Mary Todd Lincoln, who participated in a séance with the Witches of Georgetown, a mother and daughter now buried at the cemetery.

“Everybody knew somebody that had been killed or was horribly wounded for the rest of their life,” Mr. Orlikoff said of the period, adding, “So, the United States was just ripe to believe in spirits.”

It was during that time that the demon cat, known as an agent of death, was first spotted at the Capitol. During a recent interview there, Samuel Holliday, the executive vice president of the U.S. Capitol Historical Society, pointed to little paw prints left in the concrete of a small rotunda near the Senate chamber.

Mr. Holliday said people had reported demon-cat sightings before the assassinations of Mr. Lincoln and President John F. Kennedy. The grimalkin also appeared before the stock market crash of 1929, according to legend. The Post’s 1935 report went further, saying that “this furry fury invariably shows up just before a national disaster and, occasionally, before a political change in administrations.”

On a crisp night this month, a New York Times photojournalist visited the Capitol to capture the feline prints for this article. As he left, a cat walked by. It wasn’t a ghost, as far as he knew.

Mr. Holliday had his doubts about the lore. To start with, watchmen had a reputation for drinking on the job back then, he said. Ordinary cats were also a familiar presence in the Capitol; they were a cheap, effective way to kill vermin, as reflected in a 1927 Times article chronicling the lives of Mary and Dirty, two felines assigned to mice watch. An 1892 article in The Evening Star described the Capitol cats as “wild as hawks,” with yowls akin to “that of a damned soul.”

“It’s perhaps more likely that instead of some demonic presence, the paw prints were left by just a regular cat wandering through as the concrete was setting,” Mr. Holliday said.

Demonic or not, the cat is not the only spirit said to haunt the halls of Congress.

On a staircase outside the House dining room, dark splotches mark the steps. Some say they are flaws in marble, while others deem them 136-year-old blood stains from when Charles Kincaid, a journalist with The Louisville Times, fatally shot William Taulbee, a lobbyist and former Kentucky representative.

Three years before the 1890 shooting, Mr. Kincaid had written an article revealing Mr. Taulbee’s extramarital affair with a woman “who worked in the model department of the patent office,” James C. Klotter, a historian, wrote in a 1980 journal article. The journalist’s exposé ended the congressman’s political career and created a bitter feud between the two that culminated in a brawl at the Capitol that had to be broken up by Capitol doorkeepers.

Hours later, Mr. Kincaid shot Mr. Taulbee. He went on to be acquitted of murder and later resumed his newspaper career. Mr. Taulbee’s ghost, in vengeance, is fabled to have tripped reporters running up and down the building’s marble stairs ever since.

Chad Pergram, the chief congressional correspondent at Fox News, wondered if he was one such victim after he fell in 2019 while tailing Justin Trudeau, then the prime minister of Canada, through the Capitol.

“Could this be part of the mythos surrounding the ghost of William Taulbee, tripping other people and maybe even tripping me — especially on camera and especially in front of the Canadian prime minister,” Mr. Pergram said in an interview. “I don’t know. But it certainly happened, and it makes me wonder.”

Libby Tucker, a Binghamton University English professor who researches supernatural folklore, said ghost stories often reckon with the sins of history, intertwining a place’s past into the legends people share about it. The Capitol had a central place in some of the nation’s most painful chapters, she said, whether it be in war, slavery or other violence.

“Ghosts are all about unfinished business, and particularly, injustice that needs to be recognized,” Ms. Tucker said.

One such aggrieved party was John Lenthall, a construction superintendent who was feuding with an architect over how to build the ceiling of what is now the Old Supreme Court Chamber when it collapsed and killed him. So is a librarian, rumored to be Charles W. Hoffman, who is said to have left behind his ghost after hiding $6,000 in U.S. bonds behind stacks of books, according to an 1898 article in The Chicago Daily Tribune.

Mr. Hoffman haunted “the vault in the subbasement which he used to inhabit, looking vainly for the missing securities,” the story said.

Mr. Adams, who was elected to represent Massachusetts in the House after his presidency, is also believed to have unfinished business at the Capitol. Having spent his final years speaking out against enslavement, Mr. Adams in 1848 rose on the House floor — now Statuary Hall — to speak about the Mexican War, a conflict he opposed as an expansion of slavery. He suffered a stroke on the spot and died in the speaker’s office two days later, on a couch that remains in the Capitol. (It has since been reupholstered, according to the Capitol Historical Society, and remains in the suite where Mr. Adams passed away, which is now a women’s lounge area.)

According to lore, Mr. Adams’s ghost lingers in the Capitol to give the undelivered speech. Steve Livengood, the chief guide and public historian at the historical society, claimed in an interview to have seen the former president on more than one occasion.

“The fact is almost everybody who works in the Capitol feels the spirit of the people who have worked there in the past, and this is just an extension of that,” he said of their encounters.

He offered minimal detail; Mr. Livengood said Mr. Adams looked fuzzy and usually turned up while he was passing through the Capitol after having a glass or two of wine at a reception.

The Times could not find any other eyewitnesses, but that may be because, according to Mr. Livengood, the best time to see Mr. Adams is late at night, when the historian prowls the otherwise empty Capitol, free of crowds, to catch a glimpse of the dead president’s ghost.

item.title: As Midterms Near, Top Law Firms That Capitulated to Trump Are on the Sidelines
item.description:
Whenever Norm Eisen, a leader of the legal resistance against President Trump, wanted to try to hold Mr. Trump accountable over the last decade, one of his first calls was to Brad Karp, the chairman of the white shoe law firm Paul Weiss.

Without hesitation, Mr. Karp would give Mr. Eisen free legal counsel on how to best oppose Mr. Trump, and would then deploy the firm’s vast legal muscle — at no cost — to help.

“He was one of the greatest champions of voting and civil rights — and for democracy — in the country, and to have someone like that advising you, resourcing you and fighting for you was indispensable,” Mr. Eisen said.

Now, as Mr. Eisen prepares to lead a coalition that has vowed to stop Mr. Trump if he tries to interfere in the midterm elections, Paul Weiss, one of nine firms to strike deals with the administration to avoid crippling executive orders, is largely on the sidelines, according to Mr. Eisen and a lawyer with direct knowledge of the matter.

The void left by Paul Weiss is only a sliver of the impact of the deals the nine firms made with Mr. Trump early in his second term. In exchange, they pledged to do nearly a billion dollars in free legal work to causes Mr. Trump champions, casting doubt on whether they would be willing to stand up to the president.

Measuring the consequences of the deals is difficult, but the lead-up to the midterm elections offers new clues. Few of the nine firms are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check Mr. Trump and his administration’s attempts to meddle, a review of public documents and interviews with democracy advocates, election lawyers and voting rights litigators shows.

The absence of the firms has raised serious worries about whether the legal profession is equipped to respond to the administration, which has already begun to file litigation intended to sow confusion about the outcome of the election. But lawyers like Mr. Eisen say that they are just as prepared and point to a string of recent court victories as evidence of their prowess.

Some of the firms have scrubbed their websites of their storied histories working on voting rights cases. At one firm that made a deal with Mr. Trump, several lawyers are quietly volunteering to help voting rights causes, hoping that their bosses do not find out, according to a lawyer at one of the firms who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The chilling effect, the interviews show, has extended to several of the top 100 firms in the United States that did not cut deals with Mr. Trump. Fearing being targeted, they have also avoided politically sensitive cases, according to interviews.

So many of them — including ones that have made deals with Mr. Trump and those that have not — have declined to help one longtime civil rights group, the Advancement Project, that it has started an internal tracker to stay on top of all the firms declining to team up on cases.

“I’ve been told, ‘We don’t do civil rights work involving the administration anymore,’ and, ‘We don’t do voting rights work anymore,’’’ said John Powers, the legal director at the Advancement Project, which often litigates voting rights cases by joining with better-financed private firms.

Most recently, when the Advancement Project filed suit with the N.A.A.C.P. against aspects of the Justice Department’s election-monitoring plans this fall, it had to set out on its own without a private partner. (On Friday, Mr. Powers said that it had received a new offer of help.)

“It’s been a sea change,” Mr. Powers said.

In some cases, Mr. Powers added, partners at firms working with the Advancement Project pulled back their support, dropped out entirely or agreed only to help on the condition that they not be named publicly.

“All too often we’re having to find workarounds because we don’t have the support,” he said.

Mr. Powers would not name the firms because he was hoping the private support would return in the future, he said.

“The pendulum is going to swing,” he predicted.

Law firms have played a key role since the civil rights movement in checking the federal government, even though suing the government over voting and civil rights cases typically pays far less compared with representing corporations. But the chance to work on those issues pro bono became a persuasive recruiting tool for firms. It served as evidence that incoming associates could not only make a lot of money assisting companies and wealthy people, but also do good.

During elections in recent decades, associates and partners have volunteered to be stationed in swing states where they could quickly initiate legal challenges on Election Day or if there was a contested counting of the results. Firms have pledged to represent poll workers while also bringing complex legal challenges against states encroaching on voting rights.

Paul Weiss repeatedly promoted its role in a landmark 1965 voting rights case. Dozens of articles and news releases on its website laid out its work during the Trump era on voting rights and election law.

“We remain steadfast in our commitment, supporting recent voting rights actions in several courts nationally as counsel of record,” the firm wrote on its website on a page dedicated to its pro bono election rights work.

But some time after Paul Weiss, which donated more money to Democrats in 2024 than any other firm, struck the deal with Mr. Trump in March 2025, the page for voting rights was taken down, along with 30 other pages related to its work on the subject.

A search of the firm’s website for the words “voting” and “voting rights” returns just two results.

Paul Weiss and seven other firms did not respond to questions asking for examples of voting rights cases or other matters the firm is working on in opposing the administration. (One of the firms that made a deal with Mr. Trump — Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft — merged with another firm.)

Mr. Trump’s norm-breaking use of power during his first term, like child separation at the border, led many firms to use their pro bono hours to oppose the administration. His attempts to interfere with the 2020 election only established more fodder.

But the postures of the firms changed during Mr. Trump’s second term.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, firms deployed their resources to oppose Mr. Trump because they faced no cost for doing so, financially or politically.

But now firms see those cases as liabilities for their profits.

In their place, lawyers like Mr. Eisen have helped establish a network of lawyers across the country. It includes pro-democracy groups, legal nonprofits, public interest law firms and a few of the most high-profile firms, like WilmerHale, that fought back when Mr. Trump targeted them with executive orders.

Mr. Eisen, who leads the Democracy Defenders Fund, said that while the group of lawyers may be different, the quality of the legal work remains. He added that he had more than enough lawyers to counter Mr. Trump in court.

“We have not seen a single time in the past 20 months in which I did not have the resources,” he said. “The muscle is still there.”

Even if Paul Weiss or any of the firms that made deals with Mr. Trump wanted to help, Mr. Eisen said, he and his clients would not trust that they would zealously represent them, given the leverage Mr. Trump continues to hold.

At the same time, Mr. Eisen acknowledged, the attempts to hold Mr. Trump accountable could use Mr. Karp, his expertise and the army of lawyers he used to deploy.

“I miss Brad,” he said.

Aric Toler contributed reporting. Alain Delaquérière and Seamus Hughes contributed research.

item.title: Led by Trump, Republicans Close Midterms With Ugly Personal Attacks
item.description:
In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a vulnerable Republican, baselessly said his Democratic opponent “probably is grooming” children.

In Texas, Republicans have cast James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, as a “freak” and insinuated he is gay, secretly a vegan, and obsessed with transgender children because he made statements supporting them in the past.

And in Michigan, Republicans have targeted the Democratic Senate nominee, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, with Islamophobic attacks. Mr. Trump has described Dr. El-Sayed as a “vicious, violent jihadist.”

Facing a backlash over rising prices and working to overcome the president’s deep unpopularity, Republicans across the country have tarred their opponents with false, inflammatory and deeply personal attacks in the final stretch of the midterm election.

In many cases, they are following the lead of a president who has repeatedly rewritten the rules of acceptable discourse in American politics. Many of the attacks have drawn little pushback from within the party, but some Republicans say they are concerned by the trend.

“It’s awful,” said former Senator Jeff Flake, an Arizona Republican and critic of Mr. Trump. Mr. Flake, who is backing candidates in both parties in the midterms, said Republicans had gone down a darker road in their messaging: “We’ve gotten progressively more crass and crude and vulgar. But this seems to be a new level.”

The strategy risks turning off some moderate voters who see the rhetoric as over-the-top or offensive, political observers said. But it could be effective at energizing the Republican base. Democrats, who have widely condemned the Republicans’ attacks, worry the lines will land with some voters.

Democrats themselves have at times used strikingly personal attacks, often accusing Republicans of corruption. And some Democrats have imitated the president’s crude approach: Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office, for example, made social-media posts this year suggesting that various conservatives were gay.

But in the midterms the Republican attacks stand out for their viciousness.

American political campaigns have long been awash in negative and dubious attacks by both parties — in debate lines, TV commercials and stump speeches — but this bitter, hard-fought cycle may set a new standard. Some political scientists said this election season had devolved into the most negative, dark campaign in modern American history.

“I think it’s the worst,” said Christina Greer, a political science professor at Fordham University. She attributed the tone to candidates’ desire to package their message for social media, and to Republicans’ mirroring of Mr. Trump: “He’s opened a portal to the degradation of our electoral system.”

In Texas, Vice President JD Vance suggested at a rally that Mr. Talarico was gay, drawing gasps from the crowd. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Mr. Vance added, referring to Mr. Talarico’s past statements in support of transgender youth.

Mr. Talarico has a girlfriend. The attack was part of a broad effort by Republicans to portray Mr. Talarico as extreme. Mr. Trump has taken to referring to Mr. Talarico as “Talafreako.”

A spokeswoman for the National Republican Senatorial Committee suggested that Democrats had brought the attacks upon themselves. In a statement, the spokeswoman, Bernadette Breslin, claimed that Dr. El-Sayed had “pledged support” for a terrorist regime and said that “if Talarico didn’t want to be called anti-meat, he shouldn’t have announced his campaign would go vegan.”

Dr. El-Sayed has said he is loyal to the U.S. Constitution. Mr. Talarico has said he is not a vegan and that his campaign “basically” runs on barbecue.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Flake said the coarseness of some Republican attacks stemmed from a mix of desperation in the party and a mimicking of Mr. Trump. But he said he found a “silver lining” in the backlash some of Mr. Trump’s “imitators” had experienced — including in Republican criticism of a headline-grabbing attack ad in the Ohio governor’s race.

That ad came from the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor. The commercial featured the mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, who says she has not spoken to her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with raping her. The sitting governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, a Republican, called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling,” even as Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance defended it.

Former President Barack Obama, appearing at a rally in Ohio this month, said he was baffled that “the standards of behavior have gotten so low that somebody can run an ad like that.”

In Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a Republican who built a brand on civility, denounced a radio ad from the top super PAC for Senate Republicans that cast her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, as a “freak” for having two children with his second cousin. Ms. Collins called for the ad to be taken down.

But Ms. Collins, who has deplored Mr. Jackson’s efforts to cast her as corrupt, herself commented on Mr. Jackson’s family in the summer, telling Politico: “I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin.”

Other Republican attacks have gone largely unchallenged inside the party. After Mr. Marshall suggested his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, was a “groomer” of children, there was no significant Republican criticism. And there was no Republican uproar after Mr. Trump used an anti-trans slur to refer to the Democratic Senate nominee in South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews, calling her “Tranny Annie.” (Dr. Andrews is not transgender.)

A spokesman for Mr. Hamilton, Tyson Brody, said in a statement that Mr. Marshall was “resorting to increasingly unhinged and inexplicable smears.” Dr. Andrews released an ad this month in which she said she did not support transgender women playing in women’s sports or gender transition surgeries for minors. (In 2022 she had spoken out against a trans sports ban in South Carolina.)

On the campaign trail in Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for Senate, has often brought supporters who have questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to America.

At a Rogers rally in Plainwell, Mich., on Thursday, Senator Tim Sheehy, Republican of Montana, told the crowd, “You better be afraid,” suggesting that supporting Dr. El-Sayed would be a step toward Shariah law in Michigan. “We have a radical Islamist on the other side of this ticket who hates this country.”

Asked later about Mr. Sheehy’s comments, Mr. Rogers told reporters, “You haven’t heard me say any of those things.”

Dr. El-Sayed said at a rally on Sunday that Mr. Rogers’s “whole campaign is to point at me and my name and my faith.”

“But my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Islamophobic attacks have long been a feature of American politics. But in the past, candidates in both parties sought to push back. In 2008, the Republican nominee for president, Senator John McCain, defended his opponent, Barack Obama, when a woman at a rally said she did not trust him because “he’s an Arab.” Mr. McCain replied, “No, ma’am, he’s a decent family man.”

This year, Democrats say they fear that Islamophobic attacks on Dr. El-Sayed have resonated with some voters and are hurting his chances in a race that is critical in the battle for Senate control.

“I won’t say it’s the worst and most horrific ever,” Mike McGuinness, the Democratic mayor of Pontiac, Mich., said of the Republican attacks on Dr. El-Sayed’s faith and background. “But it is definitely a Hall of Fame contender.”

The Rev. Horace Sheffield III of New Destiny Christian Fellowship in Detroit said the rhetoric in the campaign felt to him as if it came from long ago in American history.

“This tenor and tone that we find ourselves in now is very dangerous,” said Mr. Sheffield, who supports Dr. El-Sayed and whose daughter is Mayor Mary Sheffield of Detroit. “And it’s all based on prejudice.”

Cayce Myers, a professor of political communication at Virginia Tech who studies negative ads, said the race in Michigan was a “test case” for how inflammatory a message could be and still help, rather than hurt, a candidate in 2026.

Negative ads typically are the most motivating, he said, and Republicans in Michigan and elsewhere appeared to be betting that their approach would help activate base voters more than it would alienate voters in the middle.

But, Professor Myers added, Republicans are “pushing up against the limit of what voters and the electorate have an appetite for.”

item.title: Republican Leads Independent in Nebraska Senate Race, Poll Finds
item.description:
Senator Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, a Republican, holds a six-point lead over Dan Osborn, the independent seeking to unseat him, according to a new poll from The New York Times and Siena University.

Many Democrats have been supporting Mr. Osborn’s bid, believing that an independent has a better chance of flipping a Republican Senate seat in Nebraska than a Democrat. But the poll found that most voters there appear to view Mr. Osborn as a Democrat in disguise.

The race is seen as a test of how independents may fare in an environment where both parties’ brands have become politically toxic.

More than half of voters — 55 percent — say they see Mr. Osborn, a union leader, as more of a Democrat than anything else. Just one third of voters say they consider him to be an independent.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Oct. 23-29

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 809 voters in Nebraska conducted Oct. 23 to 29. Question wording has been condensed.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

That perception is a challenge in a state that Mr. Trump won two years ago by more than 20 percentage points, and where views of the Democratic Party are particularly grim. Just over one quarter of voters say that they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, compared with 45 percent who say they are satisfied with Republicans. The poll found close to half of voters in Nebraska approve of the president’s job performance, which is above the national average of 37 percent.

Even independent voters are skeptical that a truly independent candidate is on the ballot. Forty-three percent say Mr. Osborn is more of an independent, while 42 percent see him as more of a Democrat. The only group that saw him as more independent was Democrats.

Many Democrats were eager to support Mr. Osborn, seeing an independent as their best hope for unseating a Republican in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in two decades. Cindy Burbank, who became the Democratic nominee for Senate, withdrew from the race in July to clear a path for Mr. Osborn, as she pledged to do during the primary.

Mr. Osborn and Mr. Ricketts each ran for the Senate two years ago, but in separate races. Mr. Osborn challenged Senator Deb Fischer, a Republican, and lost by roughly six percentage points. Mr. Ricketts ran in a special election to retain the seat he was appointed to when former Senator Ben Sasse, a vocal critic of Mr. Trump, resigned.

That year, Mr. Ricketts, a reliable Republican vote in the Senate, won by double digits. This cycle, the poll finds Mr. Ricketts up by a much narrower margin.

His race is far tighter than the battle for the governorship, where Governor Jim Pillen, a Republican, is ahead by 14 percentage points in his bid for re-election.

And while there is little publicly available polling of the Senate race, and much of it is aligned with one of the campaigns, if the Times/Siena poll underestimated Mr. Osborn’s support by even a few percentage points, it could put him in striking distance.

The poll found Mr. Ricketts ahead with traditionally Republican-leaning groups such as older voters, white working-class voters and men.

Mr. Osborn, for his part, has consolidated more than 90 percent of support among Democrats and is leading among independent voters by close to 30 points.

item.title: Talarico Makes Final Pitch to Texans: ‘You Are My Slingshot’
item.description:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, invoked the mythological grandness of his native state when he told a crowd in El Paso this week, “Our musicians are so iconic, they only need one name: Willie. Beyoncé. Selena.”

Improbable as it might seem, the once-obscure 37-year-old state representative and former middle-school teacher with the choirboy face has entered an elite pantheon himself.

A little more than a year after Mr. Talarico began his candidacy, he has become a marquee political persona, and not just in Texas. His race, which could become the most expensive in the history of nonpresidential campaigns, may well decide which party controls the Senate.

The Democratic candidate’s celebrity has thrown Republicans into a panic, prompting the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to donate an unheard-of $158 million to groups that support Mr. Talarico’s G.O.P. opponent and the state attorney general, Ken Paxton.

A smooth orator and prolific fund-raiser, Mr. Talarico has cast his upstart campaign in biblical terms. He is David, the corrupt political system exemplified by Mr. Paxton is Goliath and in whatever city he happens to be in, he declares, “You are my slingshot.” He has run a largely mistake-free campaign, although the flu took him off the trail for nine days.

He has consistently drawn overflow crowds, many of whom wear T-shirts declaring themselves to be “Talafreakos,” first deployed by Mr. Paxton as a term of derision. Last Tuesday, an estimated 4,000 people turned out in Lubbock — an extraordinary number for a Democrat in the ruby-red city — while Mr. Paxton was campaigning with President Trump less than three miles down the road.

In Texas, these count as remarkable feats for a Democrat. But because it is Texas, such accomplishments may still not be enough for victory.

“I think James has at most a 50 percent chance of winning,” said Luke Warford, the chairman of the Travis County Democratic Party. “Which, look, in Texas, that’s phenomenal. If you told me a year ago a Democrat would have a coin-flip chance of winning, I’d be doing backflips.”

People close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign privately echoed Mr. Warford’s assessment of the race. A New York Times/Siena University poll in September and a CNN/SSRS poll conducted Oct. 20 to 27 showed Mr. Talarico ahead by 6 percentage points, but other recent public surveys show him either tied with Mr. Paxton or within the margin of error with a 2-point lead. The candidate’s internal polls match those tighter surveys, people close to Mr. Talarico said, and may not be fully capturing the sentiments of rural conservative voters who support Mr. Trump.

There is plentiful evidence the race could go either way. During the homestretch of Mr. Talarico’s campaign, from deep-blue regions (San Antonio, Laredo, the Rio Grande Valley and El Paso) to steadfastly Republican terrain (Midland and Lubbock), Mr. Talarico’s bursting-to-capacity crowds made it possible to imagine that he could flip a statewide race for the first time in decades. Just as ubiquitous were signs his efforts could fall short.

A major obstacle facing Mr. Talarico is the avalanche of attack ads funded by Mr. Musk, in which the candidate is portrayed as a far-left extremist. At a stop one afternoon at the Bexar County Democratic Party headquarters in San Antonio, Mr. Talarico assured volunteers that their door-knocking work would surmount Mr. Musk’s efforts, saying, “The political science is very clear: TV ads don’t make much of a difference.”

But three days later, one of Mr. Talarico’s supporters who attended the Lubbock event, Rebecca Murrow, begged to differ when a reporter asked whether the attack ads were having an impact among people she knew. “Oh, you better believe they are,” she said.

A friend standing next to her, Luke Anderson, concurred, citing his mother as one example of a person who could not bring herself to support Mr. Talarico after viewing the ads.

Still, Ms. Morrow added, “It makes me proud to be supporting someone who’s trying to change their minds, no matter how hard it is.”

Mr. Talarico’s barnstorming tour, “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts,” is named after part of the motto of the film and TV series “Friday Night Lights,” about Texas high school football. The candidate frequently recites the lyrics of Lyle Lovett, the Texas singer-songwriter. His omnipresent footwear is not-too-shiny Lucchese cowboy boots, primarily made in El Paso. In short, Mr. Talarico has made one thing abundantly clear in every campaign appearance: He really wants you to know that he’s a Texan.

Flashing his Lone Star credentials as an eighth-generation native son is a tacit acknowledgment that the pale and slightly built pastor-in-training does not personify the Texas swagger the way the state’s political titans of yesteryear did, among them former Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson and George W. Bush and former Govs. Ann Richards and Rick Perry. (As it happens, Mr. Paxton was born in North Dakota and spent some of his youth in California, though his party does not seem to hold that against him.)

The “I’m one of y’all” references also constitute a self-normalizing effort to make up for what Mr. Talarico now terms “cringey” remarks he uttered several years ago about God being “nonbinary” and his belief that there are six biological sexes.

While those earlier statements live on in attack ads, Mr. Talarico has provided little in the way of new material for his opponent’s ad makers. He is self-disciplined, stays on script and comes off as more the seminary student he once was than the kind of fire-breathing populist fashionable in the Trump era. He wears the same youthful, Texas business casual uniform every day: a tailored blazer, a crisp white dress shirt, jeans and those cowboy boots.

Although he talks to the local media, of late he has declined most interviews with the national press, including The New York Times, on the grounds that those engagements are less likely to win votes. He travels aboard his “Talarico for Texas” R.V. with a small inner circle of young aides rather than outside political consultants. At events, his volunteers distribute signs that have his name on one side and “Love Thy Neighbor” on the other.

Projecting himself as a conciliator has helped win support from more than two dozen current or former state Republican officeholders, not to mention two relatives of Mr. Bush: his brother Neil and his daughter Barbara. A source close to Mr. Talarico’s campaign confirmed that members of the family had reached out and that the candidate has been in touch with them. That said, the Bush name no longer means what it used to in Texas, and it remains to be seen if Mr. Talarico’s throwback appeal for a kinder, gentler political culture can prevail amid a pugilistic zeitgeist.

Mr. Talarico’s trip to Lubbock pointed to the subtext of his campaign. No matter what the polls say, in Texas the underdog is by nature the Democrat. Mr. Talarico does not have the luxury of focusing his efforts on the deep-blue urban areas of the state. He is obliged to find votes everywhere he can, even in hostile territory.

In both Midland and Lubbock, Mr. Talarico’s advance staff had to scramble to find bigger places that would accommodate his crowds, then made sure to post those images on social media. Talafreakos living outside Texas contrasted what they saw with Mr. Paxton’s lackluster gatherings and asked the inevitable question: With these crowds, how can we possibly lose?

Few if any of the roughly 600 Midland Democrats standing in line for Mr. Talarico’s event suffered any such illusions. “Our Talarico lawn sign is the only one for blocks around,” said Linda Jordan, 78, a Democrat. “The neighbors don’t talk to us much.”

Tamara, a 43-year-old Midland Democrat who declined to give her last name, said of her neighbors that “there’s no changing their minds” and that her energies were instead focused on persuading her husband to vote for Mr. Talarico. She suspected, she said, that he had voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, though “he still won’t tell me.”

Mr. Talarico’s allies acknowledge that for him to win, he will need to maximize turnout in Latino-heavy communities. But Democratic Party officials said in interviews that while knocking on doors in both San Antonio and El Paso, they encountered abiding loyalty to Mr. Trump and an aversion to Mr. Talarico, particularly among Latino men. In downtown Lubbock this week, a long line of the president’s supporters waiting to get into a Trump rally included numerous Latino men, many of them wearing “Make America Great Again” caps.

Mr. Talarico’s surrogates are now couching their sense of urgency about the Latino vote in comic appeals.

In San Antonio, the actress Eva Longoria exclaimed: “Tell everyone! Tell your ex-boyfriend!” In El Paso, the city’s congresswoman, Veronica Escobar, beseeched a group of volunteer canvassers, “By all means, harass your family and your friends.”

In the end, people close to Mr. Talarico acknowledge that though Mr. Trump’s popularity has waned in Texas over the past two years, enough of his supporters remain to determine the outcome in Mr. Paxton’s favor, assuming they choose to back him.

In a last-ditch effort to split Republican loyalties, the Talarico campaign recently authorized the state party to send out mailers featuring a quote from a Texas woman: “I voted for Trump, but I cannot vote for Ken Paxton.”

Standing in line while awaiting Mr. Talarico’s arrival in Midland, Javier Soto, 59, said his father was among the many Texans who had supported Mr. Trump throughout the years. “But he says it’s time for a change,” Mr. Soto said.

item.title: Advocacy Groups Sue to Stop Trump Effort to Set Aside Ballots in Washington State
item.description:
Immigrant advocacy groups in Washington State filed suit late Friday night seeking to bar the Trump administration from forcing state election officials to set aside ballots from nearly 400 residents the administration believes may not be citizens.

The lawsuit, filed in Federal District Court in Seattle, was the latest legal move taken to stave off pressure from the White House to stop noncitizens from voting — even though the administration has often been wrong about whether registered voters are citizens.

The suit in Seattle came in response to a letter that federal prosecutors sent on Monday to Washington’s secretary of state, Steve Hobbs, demanding that he instruct election officials not to accept ballots from the 400 people until federal agencies could determine their citizenship.

Days later, Trent McCotter, the No. 2 official in the Justice Department, followed up with a second letter reminding Mr. Hobbs that mishandling ballots is a federal crime.

The suit from the advocacy groups took issue with both the accuracy of the list of voters sent to Mr. Hobbs and what it characterized as veiled threats of prosecution by senior Justice Department officials.

“Defendants’ list is not evidence of anything,” the suit maintained, “and their deeply chilling threats of federal penalty for election officials and others who fail to conform to their demands are baseless.”

Washington is not the only state that has faced heavy pressure from the Trump administration to set aside ballots from voters deemed to be ineligible because of their citizenship.

The administration sued California state officials, seeking to force them to set aside the ballots of more than 20,000 registered voters it said were noncitizens. That move was blocked for the second time on Friday by a federal appeals court, which determined that granting the government’s request would have undermined California’s authority over its election procedures and violated the “plain text” of the Constitution.

In a parallel effort, the Justice Department has issued a flurry of subpoenas to California state election officials in a widening criminal investigation seeking to prove its unsubstantiated claims that thousands of noncitizens are on California’s voter rolls.

But, in a major setback to the administration, a federal judge in San Francisco issued a ruling late on Friday blocking the Justice Department from threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with its directives on handling ballots.

The ruling, by Judge Trina L. Thompson, ordered the department not to “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials or workers to demand that they halt processing the ballots” based on the government’s suspicion that the voters might be noncitizens. She has scheduled a hearing for Monday.

item.title: Susan Collins Is Always Keeping Score
item.description:
Jordan Wood, a Democrat from Lewiston, Maine, was the first person to announce a 2026 campaign challenge to Senator Susan Collins, and he made a priority of winning the endorsement of the mayor of his hometown. He met with Mayor Carl Sheline, a fellow Democrat, in his office and over drinks at a local Italian restaurant. They had a series of phone calls. But ultimately Mr. Sheline declined to back him.

Ms. Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent, was not in the room, at the bar, or on the line.

But she had made her presence known.

Mr. Sheline had various reasons for withholding his support, he said in an interview. Among them, he acknowledged, were a housing project, a food distribution center, and a mill museum in Lewiston. Ms. Collins had helped with the finances for all of them.

“It’s just an environment of possible retribution,” Mr. Wood said. “It is that fear she instills.”

Over nearly 30 years, Ms. Collins, a self-styled moderate in a familiar Maine mold, has cultivated a public persona as a workhorse and a fastidious maestro of constituent services and pork-barrel disbursements, using her Washington know-how to get her constituents what they need.

But for just as long, her detractors say, she has managed to mostly mask another reality. “The gentlewoman from Maine,” as her colleagues say on the Senate floor, is a formidable power broker who can play a fierce brand of politics with a how-dare-you air. According to more than 40 interviews with Republicans and Democrats in Maine politics, former staff, colleagues and longtime observers, Ms. Collins has wielded power not so much as a Yankee Republican but as a shrewd machine politician.

“It’s almost like Tammany Hall,” said Amy Fried, a retired political scientist from the University of Maine. “You’re going to get this benefit here if you vote for me.”

Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist and former aide to Ms. Collins, did not disagree.

“That’s exactly what it is,” he said. “She’s openly discussing the fact that Maine is going to be set back if she’s not in that position,” he added. “It puts people in the position of very clearly understanding that voting against her is a vote against their own well-being.”

Ms. Collins’s staff stresses that she has worked to bring money back to all communities in Maine — regardless of whether they support her.

Annie Clark, a longtime aide to Ms. Collins, provided The New York Times an exhaustive list of projects, from Orono and Ogunquit to Belfast and Blue Hill, for which the senator had secured funding since 2021. The senator got $234 million for 96 projects in Cumberland and Knox counties — the only two counties she lost in 2020. In Portland, where she received just 21 percent of the vote: $51.2 million for 28 projects.

“Senator Collins has been extraordinarily effective,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins. “She works tirelessly to deliver results for the state, meets with thousands of Mainers every year, and she secures billions of dollars for communities in all of Maine’s 16 counties whether they vote for her or not.”

Ms. Collins, 73, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, is running for re-election this fall the way she always has — no clickbait TikTok posts or big, rah-rah rallies, but a relentless focus on stops in small towns where she has brought home federal dollars for boat landings, emergency operations centers and wastewater treatment facilities.

At her campaign events, supporters hold signs that underscore the point she is trying to make: “Thank You, Susan.”

In debates this month with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, a former logger and Maine Senate president, Ms. Collins was unsubtle about the crux of the deal.

“In the past five years I’ve secured $1.5 billion for properties all over the state,” she said.

She was even more blunt in a radio interview this week, citing 672 projects that she had secured across the state, including 45 new fire stations.

“All that goes away,” she said, “if Troy were to be elected.”

Her whole life has been a lesson in the accrual and use of power.

Ms. Collins was born and raised in Caribou in Aroostook County, the state’s most northern terrain. The Collinses didn’t just own and run the local lumber company and hardware store. They were politicos too.

“My parents,” Ms. Collins told The New York Times this past summer, “both served as mayor of Caribou. My father was in the State Senate, my grandfather, great-grandfather served in the state legislature.”

Her parents were supporters of William S. Cohen when he ran for Congress in 1972 and beyond, and Ms. Collins was a driver and an intern for Mr. Cohen when she was in college at St. Lawrence University in Canton, N.Y. After she graduated, she was hired as an aide and was on his staff for a dozen years, known by her colleagues and peers as a meticulous note-taker and over-preparer.

She ran for governor in 1994 when she was 41 and lost. She ran for Senate in 1996 and won. She said she would serve no more than two terms but then ran for re-election in 2002, 2008, 2014 and 2020.

Over the course of her three decades in the Senate, drafting off the renown of her cordial, consensus-building Maine forebears like Mr. Cohen and Senator George Mitchell, Ms. Collins has emphasized her image as the last of a vanishing breed. She has bucked her party, and in particular President Trump, more than enough to frustrate many Republicans — albeit not nearly enough to satisfy most Democrats.

“I’m consistently sought out by both sides for cosponsorship of bills,” she told The Times in her first year in the Senate. “I have a lot of power — I like that.”

Behind closed doors, though, she long has had a reputation as a lone wolf.

Her relationship with Olympia Snowe, the Republican who was elected to the Senate from Maine two years before Ms. Collins and served three terms, was marked by rivalries and perceived slights, according to former aides to Maine lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Publicly, they issued joint statements and often voted together. Privately, the relationship was far more fraught, as is sometimes the case when a state is represented by two senators of the same party.

“She was just hypersensitive to Olympia getting more credit than she was,” said Kurt Bardella, a former press secretary for Ms. Snowe.

“It was very machine-politicky: ‘I am owed a certain level of stature and respect,’” Mr. Bardella recalled.

Ms. Collins has a bristly relationship with Angus King, the independent junior senator from Maine, who defeated her in the governor’s race in 1994 and succeeded Ms. Snowe in 2013. While they exchange occasional text messages, the two haven’t spoken in months, according to people familiar with their communications who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private matters. They last texted Oct. 12, according to Ms. Clark. Aides in Mr. King’s office often are instructed to let Ms. Collins get the lion’s share of the credit, they said, if that’s what it takes to get a policy initiative accomplished.

When Mr. Wood announced his candidacy for Senate, he thought he knew what he needed to know about Ms. Collins. His campaign quickly became a window into what he did not know.

Elected Democrats and political donors, Mr. Wood said, told him Ms. Collins reviewed the lists of who gives more than $1,000 to whom — and kept score.

“People told me they could not give me money because they knew she would look at the report,” he said. “Democrats.”

Ms. Clark, the spokeswoman for Ms. Collins, said the senator does not review such lists.

Ultimately, Mr. Wood’s fledgling campaign was overwhelmed by the unexpected rise of Graham Platner, whose subsequent fall precipitated Mr. Jackson’s selection as the Democratic nominee. Still, he got an eye-opening tutorial in the sway of his state’s senior senator.

Last November, when he ended his Senate campaign and switched to run instead for Maine’s Second Congressional District, Mr. Wood couldn’t help but notice the difference.

This time, Mr. Sheline, the Lewiston mayor, endorsed him right away.

This month, politicking her way through the annual fall fair in Fryeburg, Maine, Ms. Collins walked from a cattle auction to a livestock barn, putting up with out-of-town press asking her questions about the president while trying to steer clear of manure.

“I know you don’t like me,” she told one reporter, “but don’t make me walk through shit.”

She quickly changed the subject — to $38 million in federal aid for heating oil.

“I was delighted,” she said, “that I was successful in expediting the funding.”

That matters a lot, said Mr. Dutson, the senator’s former aide.

“Federal money is incredibly important up here,” he said. “The choice a lot of people are facing right now is: OK, well, I can listen to the noise out of Washington or what my party tells me to do — or I can support the lady who got me a new fire truck in my 500-person town.”

In the past few weeks in Maine, as Mr. Jackson has campaigned in front of large, loud crowds alongside progressive megastars such as Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, Ms. Collins has brandished a shovel at a groundbreaking at a boat landing in Orrington and attended a grand opening of a wastewater facility in Windham.

And in the stretch run of the race, people all over the state have received targeted text messages from her campaign.

“Susan Collins delivered $33 million for Knox County …”

“Susan Collins has delivered nearly $59 million for the City of Bangor …”

“Susan Collins is delivering real results across Kennebec County — 50 projects totaling more than $109.3 million …”

Her supporters say it’s why they trust her and one of the main reasons she should be re-elected.

“What she produces is real — it’s tactile,” said Chris Gardner, the executive director of the Eastport Port Authority, who has appeared in an ad for Ms. Collins. “We should be thankful.”

Kevin Raye, a former Maine Senate president and Ms. Snowe’s former longtime chief of staff, is an anti-Trump former Republican who is now an independent — “rooting,” he said, for Democrats to take control of Congress. “But I’m in the Collins camp,” Mr. Raye said, citing her record of bipartisanship. “The thought of replacing her with a reliable partisan vote, no matter the party,” he said, “is so the wrong direction for America.”

But the calculation, her critics counter, is more complicated. Her vote to advance Mr. Trump’s big domestic policy bill before she ultimately voted against it, her initial votes against setting congressional limits to military actions in Iran followed by eventual votes to do just that — all of it costs her constituents, they say, contributing to cuts to health care and higher prices for fuel, food and more. Many remain furious about her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, a move that ultimately led to the end of Roe v. Wade.

“She’s very good at cutting ribbons,” said Betsy Sweet, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully for governor in 2018 and for Senate in 2020 against Ms. Collins. “She’s also really good at cutting your health care.”

Moreover, as she works to fend off her challenger in a tough year for Republicans, Ms. Collins’s sharp political style has been apparent not just to political insiders but to voters as well.

In a recent interview with Politico, Ms. Collins was startlingly cutting about her opponent.

“I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin,” she said. “I don’t know whether people know that or not.” They did now.

“This is a Susan people haven’t seen,” said Tony Payne, the executive director of the Republican Party of Maine in the 1970s who became an independent after the rise of Mr. Trump and a longtime critic of Ms. Collins. “This is the peeling off of the veneer.”

Last week, the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing the Republican Party’s candidates, aired a radio ad about Mr. Jackson with a crude jingle alluding to the relationship. After it had made the rounds, Ms. Collins told reporters she “had nothing to do with that ad,” saying it should be removed from the air.

This week, Ms. Collins’s campaign has been airing a TV ad that many in Maine considered elitist. “We’re not talking about a cord of wood here, we’re talking about the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective,” Bill Green, a well-known, retired local sportscaster, says in the ad.

“For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance,” Sam Patten wrote in a post on social media castigating the ad. (Mr. Patten, a former aide to Ms. Collins, pleaded guilty during the first Trump administration to failing to register as a foreign agent.)

“She’s very smart, and she works very hard,” Mr. Patten told The Times. “There’s an arrogance in everyone in Washington,” he added, “but she never showed it before. She’s always been careful not to.”

Ted O’Meara, a former aide to Ms. Snowe who also worked for Mr. Cohen alongside Ms. Collins and managed Eliot Cutler’s campaigns for governor in 2010 and 2014, described it as a sense of entitlement. “The sense that there’s nobody else that can do this job but me or do it as well as me,” he said.

He stopped himself.

“Is this on the record?” he asked.

It was.

“She’ll be pissed,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research. Tim Balk contributed reporting from Fryeburg, Maine, and Esmé E. Deprez from Caribou and Casco, Maine.
