item.title: Shooting at Spirit Halloween in California Leaves at Least One Dead
item.description:
The police are searching for a person who shot and killed a pregnant mother of four and injured six others at a Spirit Halloween in Northern California on Friday evening, the local authorities said.

The shooting, which has rattled community members, occurred as shoppers clamored for last-minute costumes on the night before Halloween. A shooter opened fire inside the holiday store at the Solano Town Center mall in Fairfield, Calif.

When police officers arrived they found seven victims with gunshot wounds, the authorities said.

Constance Hages, 31, died from her injuries, Fairfield police said in a statement on Saturday afternoon. She was pregnant, her family told detectives.

Two of Ms. Hages’s relatives, Chelaya Colbert and Charmaine Colbert, said in phone interviews that Ms. Hages had four children and had previously worked at San Francisco International Airport.

Chelaya Colbert also said Ms. Hages, her cousin, was pregnant when she died.

“I’d like to remember her as the happy lady she was,” Chelaya Colbert, who is 25 and lives in San Francisco, said. “She loved her kids.”

Ms. Hages’s mother, Capricia Colbert, declined to speak when reached by phone, asking to be left alone to grieve her daughter.

Three other victims, including two teenagers, remained in critical condition. An additional victim is in critical but stable condition, according to the police. Two other victims were treated for gunshot wounds and have since been released from the hospital.

Janet Jacobo, 36, was shopping for a costume with her three sons, ages 6, 11 and 13, on Friday evening when she heard noises she believed to be gunshots, she said in a phone interview on Saturday.

Ms. Jacobo, who lives in Fairfield, Calif., told her children to run and began searching for an exit, she said. The doors between the mall’s interior and the Halloween store were already closed for the evening she said, adding that another shopper was rallying people to break the gate open so they could get out of the store.

She fled, running alongside her elder sons and carrying her youngest child who she said was “terrified.” As they ran, she said she heard a woman scream.

The Fairfield police did not offer any information about the identity of the victims or the potential suspect in what it called a “heartbreaking incident.” Police officials declined to answer additional questions when reached for comment, but said the police were working to confirm new details about the shooting.

“This is still a very active crime scene,” the statement said. “Detectives are speaking with witnesses and diligently working to identify the suspect responsible for this horrific shooting.”

The shooting appeared to have “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect inside the Spirit Halloween store,” Fairfield police said in a statement on Saturday, adding that they were encouraging people in the area to “remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”

The store remains closed, Lori Tesoro, a spokeswoman for Spirit Halloween said in an email on Saturday evening, adding that Spirit Halloween was cooperating with local law enforcement officials in the ongoing investigation.

Ms. Jacobo, who witnessed the shooting with her children, said she no longer plans to hand out candy this evening. She has tried to calm her six-year-old son by telling him the shooting was just a “scary show at the Halloween store.”

There was also a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Madison Heights, Mich., earlier on Friday. A 21-year-old man shot another 21-year-old man multiple times in a “brief altercation” at the holiday store in the Detroit suburbs, Madison Heights police said in a statement.

The victim, who lived in Detroit, was taken to a hospital with serious injuries and later died. The two men were acquainted, the police said in the statement. The police declined to answer further questions about the episode. The suspect in the Michigan shooting is in custody.

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Trump’s Arch Faces New Legal Challenge From Virginia and D.C.
item.description:
The District of Columbia and Virginia on Saturday sued the Trump administration to block construction of the president’s planned 250-foot arch, which he wants to begin building as early as next week.

“This project is flagrantly unlawful,” the lawsuit states.

The suit accuses the Trump administration of violating the Commemorative Works Act and a section of federal law that requires the federal government to obtain specific congressional authorization before building a monument on federal land in Washington.

The plaintiffs cite the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act, which require a process of consultation and considering alternatives before rushing forward with the project. The suit also says plans for the arch violate the Height of Buildings Act, which with limited exceptions prohibits structures taller than 130 feet in the capital.

“In their rush to break ground on the arch, defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the suit states. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”

The suit was filed by Jay Jones, Virginia’s attorney general, and Brian L. Schwalb, Washington’s attorney general.

It is one of several challenging the legality of President Trump’s arch, which the president has said is for himself but top administration officials now also claim is necessary for national security.

Arlington County, which borders the site of the planned arch, also has sued, citing traffic and safety concerns. A group of Vietnam War veterans also has sued to stop construction of the arch, which would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery from the Lincoln Memorial. That lawsuit also claims the project is unconstitutional without approval from Congress.

In a statement on Saturday, a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, did not respond to the claims in the latest suit but said the arch would serve as a landmark and “gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen and all Americans alike.”

A federal judge hearing the veterans suit expressed skepticism Friday over the Trump administration’s new argument that the president’s planned 250-foot triumphal arch is needed for national security purposes.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, contended in sworn statements that even though national security was never invoked in the initial proposal for the arch, the project was now needed to keep the United States safe from drone attacks.

But on Friday, Judge Tanya S. Chutkan of Federal District Court in Washington questioned what she called the “brand-new” national security justification.

“I’m wondering about the timing of this argument,” Judge Chutkan said, before asking for more details about Mr. Trump’s plans for snipers, drones and ammunition to be stored at the arch.

“Can you give me some support?” she asked. “Can you show me any piece of paper?”

Robert N. Stander, a deputy assistant attorney general, said he could not.

The Trump administration has tried to get that suit dismissed by contending that the veterans group lacks standing.

One of the plaintiffs, Michael Lemmon, an Army veteran who served in Vietnam, testified Friday that the proposed arch, which he called a “monstrous edifice,” would interfere with the solemn way he experiences the Arlington cemetery.

The administration says the arch will be a tourist attraction, bringing up to 22,000 tourists a day to the area. Mr. Lemmon called that “disturbing and frankly disrespectful” to the families of those buried at the site.

“The pain is real for us veterans,” he testified.

In arguing that the veterans lack standing, lawyers for Mr. Trump pointed to a recent Supreme Court ruling that shot down a legal challenge to the luxury ballroom Mr. Trump is building on White House grounds after he demolished the building’s East Wing. The court ruled that the plaintiffs, a preservationist group chartered by Congress, did not have the legal grounds to sue because they were not directly harmed by the project.

The suit from the District of Columbia and Virginia appears to present different challenges for the administration by detailing a list of what they say are concrete harms from the arch’s construction. The suit cites traffic concerns and emergency response problems, as well as issues concerning the environment and historic preservation.

“The construction of the arch will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the district and Virginia,” the suit filed on Saturday states. “The arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the district has a statutory responsibility to protect. Both the construction of the arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions.”

Even so, the arch is slated to receive final approval next week from the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by allies of Mr. Trump’s. Administration officials have told one federal court that they could break ground on the project immediately after the vote of the planning commission.

item.title: Democrats File Suit Over Closed Polling Places in Rural Alaska
item.description:
As a Justice Department lawsuit challenging the presence of two U.S. Senate candidates named Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot plays out, Democrats have filed a lawsuit in Alaska accusing election officials of failing to properly operate at least 18 rural polling locations.

The complaint, filed Friday afternoon in Anchorage Superior Court, warns that several thousand voters across remote, predominantly Alaska Native communities face disenfranchisement in a state where elections are routinely decided by a few thousand or even a few hundred votes.

Given Alaska’s vast geography and the logistical hurdles voters in remote areas encounter, state law allows any qualified voter to request an absentee ballot and establishes an in-person absentee and early voting window beginning 15 days before Election Day.

In remote communities, the state relies on agreements with local municipal and tribal offices to host and staff sites where residents can cast absentee ballots in person.

The Democrats’ lawsuit alleges that state-advertised absentee-in-person voting sites across 18 rural communities either failed to open, opened late, maintained irregular hours or lacked ballots altogether. In some communities, local workers reportedly resigned without replacements, while others had not received ballots or were unaware they were supposed to host voting.

According to the complaint, some voters traveled to their designated voting location “by boat or by plane” only to be turned away.

State Senator Bill Wielechowski wrote the elections division earlier this month, noting the 18 precincts that hadn’t opened and asking for help.

In her response this week, the Alaska elections director, Carol Beecher, said 12 of the 18 sites had confirmed they were open, three had declined to open, and state officials were still trying to contact the remaining three. She emphasized the role local partners are supposed to play in rural voting, suggesting blame for the confusion about where and when to vote rested largely in the villages rather than the state elections office.

Some 82 percent of Alaska communities are not accessible by road, and the state elections office routinely struggles to ensure residents in farther-flung places can vote, with ballots sometimes arriving too late to be counted or polling sites never opening.

This time around, Democrats want the state elections office to make sure all remote polling sites are open and stay open until polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day. They also want the state to pay their attorney fees.

item.title: ‘Poop Water’ Churns a Local Election in Parched Arizona
item.description:
A ritzy Arizona enclave is facing water cuts, and the most divisive idea to offset them begins with millions of gallons of sewage. Call it affluent effluent.

The plan — which involves rigorously treating and purifying wastewater, then routing it straight to residential taps — has long been seen as critical for the future of Scottsdale, a city heavily reliant on the dwindling flow of the Colorado River.

But in recent months, Scottsdale’s wastewater recycling program has been sucked into a bitter political dispute, and its fate could hinge on the outcome of the city’s elections on Tuesday.

The Scottsdale City Council, where two seats are up for grabs, is nominally nonpartisan, but this year’s race may change the balance of power on water issues. Two candidates, both running on a right-wing platform, deride wastewater recycling as an unproven experiment. They call it “toilet to tap” or “poop water.”

A third challenger, who is backed by Democratic groups, argues that the science behind wastewater recycling is robust, citing expert support for a technology considered safe and reliable. His opponents, he says, are capitalizing on residents’ fears of contamination and downplaying the seriousness of Scottsdale’s looming water crisis.

“They’re using buzzwords and scare tactics,” Raoul Zubia, a retired banker, said of his conservative opponents, Michelle Ugenti-Rita, a former state senator, and Barry Graham, an incumbent council member.

The dispute offers a colorful preview of the ways water is becoming increasingly politicized as scarcity forces local officials across the West to make difficult decisions and embrace unconventional solutions.

Scottsdale, a city of 240,000 northeast of Phoenix, is famous for its green golf courses and red rock peaks. It is an upscale destination for bachelorette parties and bar crawls, spas and shopping malls. But in wonkier circles, the city is also known as a leader in water treatment and engineering.

Nearly all American drinking water comes from lakes, rivers, reservoirs or underground aquifers. But Scottsdale Water, a city-operated utility, has been purifying wastewater for decades through a process with many steps and even more syllables — ozonation, membrane ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis, ultraviolet photolysis. Scientists say the resulting product is among the cleanest water in the world.

The city currently sends much of the recycled water to about two dozen golf courses, which use it for irrigation. It pumps the remainder into an aquifer, where it is eventually drawn out as drinking water, a longstanding process known as indirect potable reuse.

City leaders wanted to go further, skipping the aquifer and mixing purified water with other sources before delivering it to residential taps. That’s known as direct potable reuse.

Only a few direct potable reuse facilities operate around the world, but more are in the works. Scottsdale’s would have been Arizona’s first.

But in June, with the state updating regulations and the issue turning partisan, the City Council froze funding for the project, even as neighboring Phoenix pushed forward.

Supporters were dismayed.

“You cannot choose ‘no water’ because you have unfounded fears about water quality,” said Kathryn Sorensen, a water policy expert at Arizona State University.

Ms. Ugenti-Rita would be the program’s most vocal critic if elected. The idea is “disgusting,” she said, and she is worried recycled water could make residents sick. She has also balked at the cost of infrastructure upgrades, which city staff recently estimated at more than $160 million.

“There’s a lot at stake,” Ms. Ugenti-Rita said. “We don’t want to be the next Flint, Mich. I don’t want short or long-term health effects. We have a reputation to consider.”

Mudslinging reached its peak ahead of the summer primary election, when Ms. Ugenti-Rita appeared in a social media video with the MAGA-aligned comedian Rob Schneider.

Mr. Schneider, who was in the “The Waterboy” and lives in Scottsdale, held a cup of liquid the color of a milky latte while criticizing “toilet to tap.” He referred to one of Ms. Ugenti-Rita’s primary opponents, Solange Whitehead, as “Sewage Solange.”

Ms. Whitehead, who grew up wanting to be a sewage engineer, was unfazed.

“I was pretty flattered,” Ms. Whitehead said as she sipped a pale ale made with Scottsdale’s recycled wastewater, part of a campaign to help the public overcome the “ick factor.”

Ms. Whitehead, an incumbent council member who ran on water issues, finished first in the July primary, securing another term on the board and avoiding a runoff on Tuesday. She said she was concerned that her opponents’ rhetoric will turn residents against a critical technology.

“When you rile up people against something, it spreads,” Ms. Whitehead said. “This is not a good time to politicize and to try to create distrust.”

At Scottsdale Water’s sprawling campus, Thyra Ryden-Diaz, the utility’s interim director, defended the wastewater recycling program and said sending treated water directly to taps would not differ much from what the city was already doing.

“All water is recycled,” Ms. Ryden-Diaz said. “I don’t think that people remember their third-grade water cycle graph.”

Still, she said, it would not be a panacea for Scottsdale because the city already reuses so much of its wastewater, and unless facilities are upgraded, there will not be much left to send to taps.

Scottsdale is not running out of water anytime soon, but surveys show Arizonans are concerned that state leaders aren’t doing enough to save their most precious resource. Max Vega, a 40-year-old who works in the mining industry, is one of them.

Drinking recycled wastewater “may disturb some people,” he said on a recent evening after walking his dog at a large Scottsdale desert preserve. “But if you do it the right way, under safe regulations, then so be it.”

For others, the idea is a harder sell. Corlan and Becky Fawcett, who were visiting Scottsdale for a conference, said knowing wastewater ran from their hotel faucet would not stop them from returning.

“But it might make me want to buy my water when I get here,” Mr. Fawcett said.

The couple, who live in Utah, another water-strapped state reliant on the Colorado River, acknowledged that such technology might someday come to their hometown.

“What’s the alternative?” Ms. Fawcett asked. “What’s the other option?”

item.title: El-Sayed Doesn’t Want Haley Stevens to Join Him at Sunday Event
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, said Saturday that he did not want Representative Haley Stevens, his former primary rival, to join him at a party unity event in Detroit on Sunday.

“I don’t want any distractions,” Dr. El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally in Sterling Heights, Mich., outside Detroit. He added, “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”

Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed, who have been publicly quarreling for days, were initially expected to attend the Sunday event together, part of an effort by Representatives Debbie Dingell of Michigan and James E. Clyburn of South Carolina to broker a peace between the feuding Democrats on the eve of a critical election.

It was not immediately clear if Ms. Stevens would abide by Dr. El-Sayed’s request that she stay away from the event.

Ms. Stevens, a centrist who lost to the progressive Dr. El-Sayed by less than a percentage point in a bitter August primary, had said late Friday that she had not been told that she was unwelcome at the event. She did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.

Mr. Clyburn said Saturday that he had “no idea” if Ms. Stevens would attend. An adviser to Mr. Clyburn, Antjuan Seawright, said Ms. Stevens was still invited, and rejected any notion that Dr. El-Sayed could pull her invitation.

“This is not Abdul’s event,” Mr. Seawright said Saturday afternoon, adding, “The invitation still stands.”

Ms. Dingell, who had said Friday that she had secured the participation of Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Stevens at the event, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

Politico previously reported that Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign did not want Ms. Stevens at its events.

Dr. El-Sayed did not say at the rally in Sterling Heights whether his campaign had relayed the request directly to Ms. Stevens.

A schedule for the Sunday event, at a church in the North End of Detroit, said that speakers would include Mr. Clyburn, Dr. El-Sayed and Mayor Mary Sheffield of Detroit. Their remarks were set to be followed by a march to the offices of the Detroit Election Department, the schedule said.

Ms. Stevens was not listed as a speaker, though there was no indication she had ever been expected to deliver remarks.

Opinion polls show that Dr. El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, are locked in a tight race that could determine control of the Senate.

Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed differ over their positions on Israel. Ms. Stevens is a strong supporter of the country, and Dr. El-Sayed is a fierce critic.

Their unusual clash has become a flashpoint in Democrats’ broader debate about Israel, and some Democrats are anxious that infighting in the final days of the race will damage Dr. El-Sayed’s chances.

His relationship with Ms. Stevens was not always so tense. Ms. Stevens quickly endorsed Dr. El-Sayed after the primary, pledging to campaign with him, and they appeared together at a unity breakfast two days after the primary.

But they have not been seen together in the final stretch of the race, and Ms. Stevens made a series of recent appearances on cable TV in which she criticized Dr. El-Sayed’s outreach to Black and Jewish voters, two groups that Mr. Rogers has aggressively courted.

Ms. Stevens said in an interview Friday that she had been set off by a moment in a debate this month in which Dr. El-Sayed declined to answer a question about whether Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States.

On Wednesday, Ms. Stevens said she would not campaign with Dr. El-Sayed again before the election, and her fiancé, Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat, said he was backing Mr. Rogers, citing Dr. El-Sayed’s positions on Israel.

Ms. Dingell, frustrated by the intraparty conflict, said she reached out to the warring Democrats and Mr. Clyburn, one of the highest-ranking African Americans in Congress, and asked them to appear together. By Thursday night, Ms. Stevens was saying that she would join Dr. El-Sayed at the event on Sunday.

But the efforts to make peace crumbled Friday, after Ms. Stevens issued a statement calling on Dr. El-Sayed to apologize for comments he had made about Israel and to denounce an ad from an outside group that suggests U.S. aid to Israel was making life in America more expensive. (The ad shows a shopper telling a man not to buy eggs because “we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.”)

Dr. El-Sayed responded to Ms. Stevens’s statement with a statement of his own saying that she seemed “intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” He called on her to “focus on the task at hand.”

On Saturday, Dr. El-Sayed told reporters that he did “not agree with the contents” of the ad from the outside group. But he also said she wanted to “talk about” issues that he did not want to focus on in the final days of the campaign.

As of Friday, Mr. Turkish said he planned to attend the church service.

On Saturday afternoon, he said he wanted to spend Sunday “however my fiancé, Haley, wants to spend her day.”

But, he added, he did not know if that would include the service.

item.title: Women Voters: The Silent Democratic Majority
item.description:
In the scramble to understand where America’s head is politically this election season, the focus has been on the working class, on Hispanics and on young men. But the country’s single biggest demographic group — women — is still the main driver of voting and in this election is looking more Democratic than ever.

Women have been the backbone of the Democratic base for decades and vote overwhelmingly for Democrats most years.

In 2022, support dipped slightly, when 48 percent of women chose Democrats and 41 percent supported Republicans. But this year, support looks set to return to more typical results, with 56 percent of women saying they prefer Democratic candidates, compared with 37 percent who say they prefer Republican ones, according to New York Times/Siena University surveys.

Women are a potent political force because they vote at higher rates than men.

And this year, they are bringing a lot of energy to volunteer and get-out-the-vote efforts.

Lynda Hoving, a retired appraiser and longtime volunteer for the Democratic Party in Kent County, Mich., has been sending postcards and working the phones for Democrats.

She watched as her West Michigan county, home to Gerald Ford and a tradition of Republicanism, went from solidly red in the 1970s, when she and her husband moved there, to reliably blue in more recent political cycles.

“I was always trying to turn something from red to purple,” said Ms. Hoving, who spent years in Grand Rapids stuffing envelopes, door-knocking and making spreadsheets. “It has been my goal for my whole political life.” She said it was disproportionately the women in the county who “kept the balls rolling” for the slow, tedious work of local politics.

Now 73, she said she still reminded everyone to vote during election season, including, most recently, her orthodontist, who told her he had voted for Trump but was not happy with the way things had turned out.

But she didn’t get to try to pitch him on Democrats.

“Then they put the plastic in my mouth, and I couldn’t talk anymore,” she said. “That’s one way to force a Democrat to listen.”

Pat Smithson, 69, of Lenexa, Kan., has volunteered so much for Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Kansas, that he called out her name when he walked into a campaign event on Saturday morning. She had brought cinnamon rolls freshly baked by her daughter.

Ms. Smithson, a retired fund-raiser, has been calling voters all over Kansas since June and said that even her daughter, a Republican who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, planned to vote for Mr. Hamilton, too. “She listened to him on TV,” Ms. Smithson said. “She watches me volunteer, setting the example.”

Some of the shift away from Republicans among women in recent years has been driven by Donald Trump.

Annette Hunt, 58, who works in finance and lives in Dallas, grew up in a staunchly Republican family in East Texas.

“Reagan was almost like a God in our house,” she said.

She said she voted straight ticket Republican for most of her life. Then came Mr. Trump.

She thought he would be “like Ross Perot — a businessman who shook up the Republican Party a bit,” but she couldn’t bring herself to vote for him, so she wrote in her father, who died that year. She has always regretted it, and ever since has voted Democratic to “stop the current agenda of the Republican Party.”

Last Saturday, she voted early for James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas. She said she did not feel at home in the Democratic Party either, despite voting for their candidates for the past 10 years.

“I’m a person without a party,” she said.

Jeanne Russell, 77, who owns a farm on Verona Island, Maine, said she grew up in a Republican household but was shaped by the politics that defined her young adulthood and ended up a liberal.

“I was a child of the ’60s and ’70s,” she said. “I was aware of the injustices in the country. It bothered me. So I’ve always been a Democrat.”

She said she has never missed an election.

Murray Carpenter contributed reporting.

item.title: Newsom Warns California’s Top Courts About Election Interference
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Saturday warned the state’s top judges that the Trump administration may try to seize midterm election ballots as a legal battle continued over unproven federal claims that noncitizens are voting in huge numbers in California.

“I have grave concerns federal agents will seek search warrants to seize ballots and ballot materials before the election results are certified,” the governor wrote in an extraordinary “alert” to the four U.S. District Courts that cover California.

He added: “Indeed, the only reason to do so would be to interfere in a State’s lawful counting of ballots and certifying the results of the election.”

The warning came as the Trump administration is also claiming that there are more than 20,000 California voters who are “likely noncitizens" — an assertion that state election officials have firmly rejected.

On Saturday, data scientists analyzing that list of voters said in a court filing that it contains thousands of errors.

Mr. Newsom’s concerns about the seizure of voting machines or ballots are not unfounded.

In January, federal agents executed a search warrant at an election center in Fulton County, Ga., hauling away boxes of ballots in an effort to discredit Mr. Trump’s defeat in the 2020 election. The warrant in Fulton County was approved by a federal magistrate judge even though it was based on a series of debunked conspiracy theories about the contentious 2020 presidential race.

Ever since, election officials have worried that the Justice Department might try something similar in different jurisdictions, especially during the highly fraught days after the midterm elections.

Those concerns have not been assuaged, as Mr. Trump himself has warned that the country’s voting machines are vulnerable to foreign meddling. The president has also said that he regretted not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election.

Mr. Newsom is not the only public figure who has expressed concern that the Trump administration might resort to seizing ballots or voting machines.

On Tuesday, two former federal judges issued an unusual public statement to their working colleagues, warning them to use extreme caution before taking the “uniquely serious” step of granting prosecutors a warrant for seizures.

“Unlike the execution of a search warrant for contraband such as drugs or for the records of a criminal enterprise, executing a search warrant for ballots or voting machines before an election is certified would cause irreparable harm to a vital public process: our elections,” the former judges, J. Michael Luttig and Nancy Gertner, wrote.

Mr. Newsom’s letter to the judges was issued on the same day two data scientists from University of California, Los Angeles, released their findings of an analysis of the list of the 20,000 registered voters in California the Trump administration has claimed are not eligible to vote because they are not citizens.

The analysis — contained in court papers filed in district court in Washington by immigration advocates — found that more than 40 percent of the people on the list do not appear on the California state voter rolls. The analysis also found that the list contained thousands of people who appear to be citizens.

The scientists conducted their study by comparing the government’s list of suspected noncitizens with lists of people who had obtained citizenship. They did so with the help of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights of Los Angeles, a major California nonprofit colloquially known as CHIRLA.

The administration sued California seeking to force state officials to set aside any ballots cast by the 20,000 voters. But a federal appeals court has twice shot down that effort, saying it would rob the state of its authority to administer the election and violate the “plain text” of the Constitution. In between that court’s rulings, a district court in Los Angeles also rejected the administration’s request.

In his letter, Mr. Newsom wrote that, while he was not aware of any such pending application, “the tactics and rhetoric federal officials are using strongly suggest that, having lost repeatedly in federal civil proceedings thus far, they will quickly pivot to the criminal forum.”

The letter included a nonpartisan guide for evaluating search warrant applications that the judges could distribute to lower level federal magistrates.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed Does Not Want to Talk About Haley Stevens. Everyone Else Does.
item.description:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed had just finished his stump speech, complete with jokes about his name and exhortations to “show just how big we are” by turning out voters on Election Day. Then he walked into a room full of reporters wanting to ask about the one topic he wished not to discuss.

Representative Haley Stevens.

The first question came from a local reporter, who asked if Dr. El-Sayed believed Ms. Stevens, the congresswoman he defeated in the Senate primary who has been on a media tour criticizing his views on Israel, was trying to damage his campaign.

“That is not a question for me,” Dr. El-Sayed said, with a laugh that seemed to be a response to the crude term, including the word “rat,” that the questioner used to describe political sabotage.

The next question: Would Dr. El-Sayed do as Ms. Stevens demanded and disavow an online advertisement produced by one of Dr. El-Sayed’s allies blaming U.S. policy toward Israel for the price of groceries and health care?

Dr. El-Sayed was no longer amused.

“I’ve already been clear that that ad was not made by me, and I do not agree with the contents of that ad,” he said.

He did not wish to talk more about Ms. Stevens. If the next question was about her or the ad she wished he’d disavow, Dr. El-Sayed said he would stop taking questions and walk out.

Throughout the 12 minutes he spoke with reporters, Dr. El-Sayed never said Ms. Stevens’s name. Once he referred to her as “the congresswoman.”

He fielded a few questions about the Detroit church service he planned to attend Sunday with Representative James E. Clyburn of South Carolina and his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers.

But soon he got back to Ms. Stevens.

Why, he was asked, shouldn’t he address the issues she raised, which are also of concern to some Michigan voters? Dr. El-Sayed said the primary was over.

“We had a primary, right? And the outcomes of the primary are what they were,” he said. “I understand that some folks are upset about that. I get it. But I’m here trying to beat Mike Rogers.”

Then: Did he still want Ms. Stevens to come to church with him Sunday, as his campaign first alerted Thursday and as she said Friday that she would?

Dr. El-Sayed said he did not want “distractions.” Ms. Stevens, he said, “wanted to talk about other things” beyond his campaign’s core themes.

Translation: She wants to talk about Israel and he does not.

Finally, Dr. El-Sayed was asked a version of the first question. Had Ms. Stevens hurt the Democratic ticket by speaking out against his campaign?

He said she does not matter, and that he does not think much about her.

“It’s not really of relevance to Michigan voters. Most people don’t care about this,” he said. “I just don’t spend much of my time thinking about these sort of personality issues. Like, I have much respect to the congresswoman. We had a hard-fought primary. That primary ended in August. I’m focused now on beating Mike Rogers.”
